newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian state faces native title impasse.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian state faces native title impasse.

text.p: Australia's Queensland government is facing a shutdown in mining exploration as it battles to find answers to a controversial legal ruling that has raised land ownership fears throughout the northern state.
All exploration permits have been stopped as miners and farmers digest a High Court ruling that Aboriginal land claims can co-exist with pastoral leases held by farmers and miners.
"Advice to me from the Crown Solicitor this morning is that up to 85 percent of Queensland could be subject to native title," Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge said on Thursday.

The impasse, which has seen suspension of the issue and renewal of most mining leases in Queensland and the indefinite freezing of all land dealing and development of leasehold property, follows the court ruling last month on native title.
That decision followed an appeal by two Aboriginal groups, the Wik and Thayorre tribes, against an earlier Federal Court ruling that pastoral leases extinguished native title.

Since the national Native Title Act came into operation at the beginning of 1994, Queensland and all other states had assumed -- until the Wik decision -- that the Federal Court decision was the law of the land.
Now the High Court has ruled that native title can co-exist with state pastoral leases held by farmers and, in many cases, mining companies which have mine leases on pastoral leases.

Native title claims have already caused extensive delays for the state's biggest mining project, the A$1 billion Century Zinc mine, formerly owned by RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd which this month sold it to Pasminco Ltd.
The sale and development of Century is still conditional on a successful outcome to native title claims currently being negotiated by Century Zinc with local Aboriginal groups.
MIM Holdings Ltd's A$350 million Ernest Henry copper-gold project in north Queensland is also subject to native title claims.
"The mine lease was granted prior to 1984 and is safe. As far as the surrounding areas are concerned, we are in the same boat as everyone else," an MIM spokesman said.

A national meeting next week in Cairns, attended by farmers, miners and Aboriginal groups to try to find a compromise, is not expected to bring a quick solution, Queensland Mining Council executive director Michael Pinnock told Reuters.
"That will be a seminar only - the Federal government has not been invited officially and it has to be a national solution," Pinnock said.
He said 800 mining leases had been issued since 1994 in Queensland with the QMC calling for immediate intervention by the Federal government to solve an increasingly complex problem.
Queensland Minister for Natural Resources, Howard Hobbs said earlier "all land administration and natural resource matters in Queensland have virtually come to a halt."

Borbidge said he agreed with Hobbs' assessment of the situation and was holding top-level talks at the weekend with his counterparts in the Northern Territory and Western Australia - two other parts most affected by possible native title claims.
This would be ahead of urgent talks next week with Prime Minister John Howard to find a legislative solution, he said.
Pinnock said the QMC had no figures on how much the state's mining industry could potentially lose or how many miners had been affected by the suspension of mining lease renewals.
"Our first and foremost concern is to validate any title that has been issued since 1994," Pinnock said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
